newsitem.title: INDIA: India PM can sleep easy despite Hindu party's gain.
newsitem.headline: India PM can sleep easy despite Hindu party's gain.

text.p: Hindu nationalists have gained a new stronghold in India's most populous state, fanning their hopes of eventually winning power in New Delhi.

But analysts said on Thursday that Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda can breathe easy despite his rivals' gains because his reluctant but crucial ally, the Congress party, will now be hard pressed to withdraw support for the federal government.
"I don't see any threat to the Deve Gowda government," political analyst Rasheed Talib told Reuters.

The right-wing Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) said on Wednesday it had agreed with a party of lower-caste Hindus to form a government in Uttar Pradesh state that, with 140 million people, is more populous than Japan or Pakistan.

The northern state, which is bisected by the mighty Ganges River, has been under direct rule from New Delhi since inconclusive local elections last September failed to produce a clear majority for any one political group.

Under a novel power-sharing experiment, the BJP will allow the rival Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP) to head the two-party coalition government for six months, followed by a six-month turn at the helm by the BJP.
"The power-sharing agreement is a healthy democratic move which is likely to be increasingly resorted to in India," said Ashis Nandy of the Centre for the Study of Developing Societies.

The surprise political developments have no direct bearing on the federal government in New Delhi, ruled by the 15-party United Front coalition grouping free-traders, communists and others under the banner of secularism.
Deve Gowda's minority United Front and Congress, which gives critical backing in the federal parliament, claim the BJP favours India's majority Hindus at the expense of Moslems.
Congress President Sitaram Kesri called the tie-up in Uttar Pradesh an "unholy alliance".
Uttar Pradesh is India's biggest political plum. The state sends 85 legislators to the 545-member lower house of the federal parliament.
Seven of India's 12 prime ministers, including Jawaharlal Nehru and Indira Gandhi, have come from the state, which is bigger than France.
Congress, which has ruled India for all but four years since independence in 1947, has traditionally drawn its strength from the fertile plains of Uttar Pradesh.
The BJP-BSP alliance was a setback for Deve Gowda's defence minister, Mulayam Singh Yadav, whose Samajwadi Party had hoped to cobble together a majority in the 425-seat Uttar Pradesh state assembly.
Together, the BSP and BJP have 243 assembly seats.
The BJP, which joined with a pro-Sikh ally to win recent elections in the northern state of Punjab, sees Uttar Pradesh as a potential stepping stone to national power.

The BJP, which says India's unifying force is its Hindu culture, is the biggest single party in the federal parliament. It held national power for 12 days in May, but failed to woo enough allies to form a majority government.
Despite its reputation as a high-caste Hindu party, BJT's alliance with the BSP has attracted many Moslems.

"The BJP has an interest in bringing the intermediate castes into the fold and changing its social structure," Talib said. "The BJP is hoping that the BSP and its new look might help it in national elections if the alliance holds."
But Deve Gowda need not worry, Nandy said.

"I think Deve Gowda will not be unhappy because he will see in this a kind of clear indication that Congress will now have to wait longer to make any political bid for power-sharing. Congress will be even less eager to go to the polls."
